catalog_quote: [van Dam p. 241] Figure 9.2 shows the main features of the first three tone categories in Tutsa. Fourth tone is a checked tone, with short duration relative to other tonemes, and an oral or glottal stop coda. What follows is a very early preliminary description. A number of segmental combinations have not been adequately recorded, and nothing has been recorded within carrier sentences. Contours in Tutsa differ considerably from many other Tangsa-Nocte varieties. [...] It is still a four-tone system and the etyma fall under the same category as with other Tangsa-Nocte varieties discussed here. [...] no time was able to be spent discussing topics such as intonation or sandhi. Instead, I am only able to give a basic overview of the tonemes here. [p. 243] In the case of Figure 9.9 for ‘new’, a nominalising prefix /e0/ is present. As with other varieties, this is a toneless sesquisyllabic affix and, and, like other varieties with one or two exceptions, it does not appear to significantly alter the tone of the stem. [p. 94, on the group:] The same applies to most Tangsa-Nocte varieties. The presyllable is toneless and unstressed [...] [Sudhakaran ch. 1 p. 12] There is no existing literature to claim tones in Tutsa. However, according to this study, Tutsa has two tones (high and low) and has been marked according to the International Phonetic Alphabets (IPA).
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

The quoted passage is present verbatim: 'Figure 9.2 shows the main features of the first three tone categories in Tutsa. new_statements.rule_in_words: Tutsa is described as a lexical tone language with four tonemes (tone 1 mid falling with final breathiness, tone 2 high level, tone 3 mid/low falling, tone 4 checked/short with stop coda) on monosyllabic stems; nominalising prefixes /e0/, /a0/ are toneless minor (sesquisyllabic) syllables. The source says nothing about word stress: no stress rule, no claim of absence of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. For tone: author flags the description as very preliminary (one primary consultant plus 2013 recordings of a second speaker), no carrier-sentence data, intonation and sandhi not studied.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms (single words in elicitation, no carrier sentences); tone-bearing unit is the stem syllable; prefixes are toneless minor syllables. Nothing on phrase-level prosody for Tutsa.
new_statements.identity_note: van Dam's Tutsa data (glottocode tuts1235, ISO tvt) come from Mr. Tesam Pongte (primary consultant) and 2013 recordings of Mr. Ngongling Hanphuk of Thamjang village near Changlang Town, Changlang District; van Dam & Rahman 2022 sample Tutsa at Dewin and Hanphuk villages. Rekhung 1992 is noted by LaPolla as covering the Sabban area of Changlang Subdivision. Tutsa was administratively counted under Tangsa until the 2011 census (and under Nocte earlier, per Das 2022); linguistically van Dam places it closest to Nocte and to Phong (Ponthai) within a Tangsa-Nocte-Tutsa-Ollo continuum.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement's reading (tone language, no stress statement): Sudhakaran confirms lexical tone and is silent on stress, exactly as van Dam 2023 is. It refines nothing on stress. It does contradict van Dam on the number of tones (two vs four categories), which is a tone-inventory disagreement, not a stress disagreement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis describes Tutsa as a two-tone language (high vs low) with lexical minimal pairs and says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence anywhere in its 180 pages. Phonology is confined to sec. 1.2.1-1.2.4 (consonants, vowels, typology, tones, pp. 8-12). The only occurrence of 'stressed' is the semantic gloss marárá 'some (stressed)' for a relative quantifier (ch. 4, printed p. 51), not a phonological statement; 'stress' also appears once in the acknowledgements in its everyday sense.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress rule stated); note the thesis's two-tone inventory differs from van Dam 2023's four tone categories for Tutsa
new_statements.identity_note: Sudhakaran's thesis describes Tutsa as spoken in Changlang district, Arunachal Pradesh (fieldwork-based, Tezpur University), without naming a sub-dialect; van Dam's Tutsa data (sec. 9.2) is likewise the Arunachal Tutsa variety of the Tangsa-Nocte continuum. Both are the same language as catalog item tuts1235.

sources.citation: van Dam, Kellen Parker. 2023 [submitted 8 Oct 2018]. The tone system of Tangsa-Nocte and related northern Naga varieties. PhD thesis, La Trobe University. xviii+315 pp. (333 pp. PDF). doi 10.26181/21858474.v1
sources.note: Section 9.2 'Tutsa' (pp. 240-245) is a self-described 'very early preliminary description' of Tutsa tone only: four tones (1 mid falling breathy, 2 high level, 3 mid/low falling, 4 checked/short with oral or glottal stop coda); nominalising prefix /e0/ and /a0/ described as toneless sesquisyllabic affixes; intonation and sandhi not studied. No mention of word stress or accent for Tutsa anywhere in the thesis (the only 'stress' remarks, pp. ~140, concern emphasis/intonation in Muishaung).

sources.note: Tangsa-Nocte tonogenesis derives from proto-language phonation distinctions with no role for aspiration/voicing; a direct tone correspondence holds between Tangsa-Nocte and Wancho (and Phom), while Southeast Patkaian (Lainong, Khiamniungan) correspond only once voicing and aspiration are considered; Khiamniungan lacks the checked-tone category; argues for distinct tonogenetic events across Patkaian.
